task.goal: Develop a small museum display that makes a damaged everyday object meaningful without inventing its history.
hard_constraints: One display case, 150 words of label space and two weeks of staff time.
Unknown provenance must be marked as unknown; no fabricated owner story.
Compare visitor understanding and discomfort with a plain factual label.
task.available_resources: Object inspection notes and a curator interview.
task.expected_result: A responsible display concept and test.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Damage as a way to look
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Make the object's physical damage the reason to look closely. In the single case, position the object so one or two documented damaged features are visible without handling or treatment. A label of no more than 150 words directs attention to those features, explains their effect on ordinary use only where supported by inspection, and states: “Provenance and ownership history: unknown. The cause and date of this damage are unknown.” Separate observation from interpretation explicitly. End with a grounded invitation: “What does this damage let you notice about how the object was made or used?”

The mechanism is close observation: a familiar object becomes meaningful through its material construction and vulnerability, without needing a personal biography. Inspection notes supply the facts; the curator interview identifies what can responsibly be explained. This assumes the damage is visible and there is at least one accessible observation worth communicating. Damage alone cannot establish neglect, poverty, affection, or repair intentions. If the notes do not support an account of function, omit it.

One staff member drafts the label and prepares the case during week one; the curator checks every interpretive claim. Use week two for a visitor check and revision. No restoration, additional objects, or new historical research is required.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Alternate the interpretive label and a plain factual label in the same case across several short, balanced time blocks. Keep object position, typography, and label length similar. Invite a small convenience sample, aiming for 12 visitors per version. Ask what they noticed, what is known about the object's past, and whether any suggested history is certain; then ask for discomfort on a five-point scale and its reason. Code answers against the inspection notes. The concept fails its initial check if visitors notice no more supported detail, infer an owner story more often, or report greater discomfort without improved understanding. Treat results as formative, with visitor mix and small numbers limiting conclusions.

DIRECT_FULL.title: An object with an honest boundary
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Organize the case label around three explicit categories: “Observed,” “Possible,” and “Unknown.” Within the total 150-word allowance, give two or three observations drawn from the inspection notes, at most one useful interpretation supported by the curator interview, and a clear statement that provenance, ownership, and any undocumented cause of damage are unknown. If no interpretation is adequately supported, omit “Possible” rather than fill it with speculation. Display the object so visitors can check at least one observation themselves.

The mechanism is making the museum's evidential limits visible. The damaged everyday object becomes meaningful as an encounter with how knowledge is built and where it stops. Visitors can recognize that an institution's uncertainty is information, rather than a gap requiring an invented biography. This approach assumes the notes distinguish physical observations from deductions and that the curator can explain that distinction in ordinary language. It may feel procedural or emotionally distant; category headings alone will not guarantee understanding.

During week one, a staff member extracts claims from the notes and interview, assigns each a category, and asks the curator to challenge the assignments. Produce a simple printed label and install it beside the object in the existing case. Reserve week two for comparison and editing. The concept needs no visitor contributions, added collection material, or external research.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare this label with a plain factual label containing the same established object facts and the same explicit provenance disclosure. Alternate versions in balanced time blocks. Aim for 12 brief visitor interviews per version. Ask visitors to identify one observation, one uncertainty, and whether a suggested cause of damage is established; ask them to rate discomfort and explain it. Also ask whether the display helped them understand why the object deserves attention. Reject or revise the concept if headings increase confusion, speculation is recalled as fact, or evidential understanding improves only by making the object seem less worth viewing. These are exploratory responses, not proof of a general effect.

DIRECT_FULL.title: The visitor supplies the association
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Use a personal reflection prompt to connect the object to ordinary life while keeping its own biography explicitly unknown. The single case holds the object and a label of no more than 150 words. Begin with supported identification and visible condition, then state: “Its provenance and ownership history are unknown. We do not know how this damage happened.” Follow with: “Think of an everyday object whose damage changed how you saw it. Does that experience change what you notice here? Your association belongs to you; it is not evidence about this object's past.” Do not collect or exhibit visitor stories.

The mechanism is autobiographical association: visitors bring significance from their own experience rather than receive an invented owner narrative. It assumes that the object's everyday function is recognizable or can be explained from available evidence. It also assumes visitors can distinguish their associations from historical claims. The prompt may evoke loss, financial hardship, or distress, so participation stays optional and asks for no disclosure. Meaning may vary substantially, and some visitors will prefer factual interpretation.

In week one, use the inspection notes to establish the factual opening and the curator interview to check wording, accessibility, and unintended emotional pressure. Print the label and install it with the object; use week two for a small comparison and revision. No audio, response station, additional objects, or ongoing moderation is needed.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Alternate the reflection label with a plain factual label in the same case, retaining the same factual opening and unknown-provenance statement. Aim for 12 visitors per condition across balanced time blocks. Ask what made the object meaningful, what they believe is known about its history, and whether the display prompted an unwanted personal memory. Collect a five-point discomfort rating without asking visitors to describe private experiences. The concept fails its initial check if visitors attribute their imagined stories to the object, report pressure to disclose, or show no greater sense of significance while discomfort rises. Report the range of reactions and uncertainty rather than treating average engagement as sufficient evidence of success.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Does damage disqualify an object?
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Make the object the focus of a curatorial judgment: can something damaged deserve museum attention? The mechanism is a change in the visitor’s role, from receiving an account to evaluating a collecting principle. Everyday usefulness and museum significance can differ; visitors consider that distinction without supplying a missing owner biography.

Use one case, with the object safely positioned and a single label under 150 words. Begin with identification and condition supported by the inspection notes. State: “Provenance and ownership history: unknown. Any undocumented date or cause of damage is also unknown.” Then ask: “Should damage count against an object’s place in a museum? Consider what this example can show and what its missing history prevents us from saying. You may decide that it deserves a place—or that the available evidence is insufficient.” Include one concise, curator-approved reason for displaying this particular object, explicitly presented as the museum’s present judgment.

This requires the curator interview to yield an honest selection rationale grounded in the object’s documented features. If no such rationale emerges, the concept is unsuitable. It does not establish rarity, representativeness, or historical importance. Its limit is that visitors may attend more to museum policy than to the object.

During week one, one staff member extracts the facts, interviews the curator, drafts the label, and obtains a claim-by-claim review. Use existing mounting and printed labels; reserve week two for visitor comparison and revision. No additional objects, research, or response installation is required.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Alternate this label with a plain factual label across balanced short time blocks, keeping the same object position, established facts, and uncertainty disclosure. Aim for 12 brief interviews per version. Ask what the object demonstrates, what remains unknown, and why a museum might display it. Record whether explanations use supported features or invented history. Ask for discomfort on a five-point scale and an optional reason. Revise or abandon the concept if visitors merely repeat the question, invent biography more often, or feel judged for their answer without improved understanding. Treat this small convenience sample as formative evidence.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Care happening now
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Make the museum’s present care of the object the display’s subject. A damaged everyday object becomes meaningful through a visible act of protection: visitors see how its condition changes what people must do for it now. This offers a documented present relationship without inventing a past owner.

Use the inspection notes and curator interview to identify one actual, condition-specific display decision—for example, supporting a weakened area or choosing an orientation that avoids pressure on a fracture. These are possibilities to verify, not facts to assume. Position the object safely in the single case so visitors can see the relevant feature and, where practical, its support. Do not deliberately expose it to risk for demonstration.

Within 150 words, identify the object using supported facts, explain the verified care decision in ordinary language, and state: “Provenance and ownership history: unknown.” Explicitly mark any undocumented cause or date of damage as unknown too. Connect the decision to its immediate purpose: what further damage the support is intended to prevent. Avoid claiming that the object was treasured, neglected, or repaired by an earlier owner.

The prerequisite is an existing or readily achievable care decision that the curator can substantiate within their expertise. If safe installation requires specialist assessment or a new custom mount beyond available resources, this concept is unsuitable. In week one, one staff member reviews the notes, interviews the curator, drafts the label, and prepares the approved installation using existing materials. Week two covers visitor checks and revision. The principal uncertainty is whether visitors find present care meaningful or merely technical.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Keep the safe installation identical while alternating the care label and a plain factual label across balanced short periods. Both labels include the same identification, condition facts, and unknown-provenance disclosure. Aim for ten brief visitor interviews per version. Ask what the damage changes about displaying the object, what remains unknown about its history, and what, if anything, makes it worth attending to. Record a five-point discomfort rating and an optional explanation, including whether the presentation feels overly sentimental. Revise or reject the concept if visitors cannot explain the care decision more accurately, infer earlier affection or ownership more often, or report increased discomfort without improved understanding. Treat this small sample as a formative check, not a reliable population estimate.

EXPAND.title: A familiar task interrupted
EXPAND.proposal:
Make the object meaningful through a practical question: what happens when an ordinary tool can no longer complete its job? In the single case, pair the object with a label of at most 150 words that explains one documented everyday function, invites visitors to mentally attempt that task, and identifies how the documented damage would affect it. State explicitly: “Provenance and ownership history are unknown. The date and cause of the damage are unknown.” Describe a consequence of the present condition, never an event in a former owner's life.

The mechanism is mental simulation of interrupted use. Visitors encounter the object's significance through the work it enabled and the consequence of losing that capability. Unlike the prior close-observation route, the intended outcome is understanding a practical dependency, rather than noticing more physical detail. Whether this produces greater meaning remains uncertain.

This requires inspection notes that support both the function and the damage's functional consequence. During the first two days, a staff lead extracts those claims and asks the curator to check them. If the consequence cannot be established without handling, testing, or speculative reconstruction, stop this route. Do not demonstrate use with the damaged object. Complete a paper label prototype and curator review in week one; use week two for the visitor comparison and revision. No additional objects, treatment, or external research are needed. The prompt must remain answerable from the display, without assuming specialist knowledge. If visitors mistake the simulated task for an actual historical incident, remove the simulation and return to the factual label.
EXPAND.experiment: The staff lead alternates three labels in balanced short blocks: plain facts, the prior close-observation approach, and interrupted use. All fit the 150-word limit and retain identical provenance disclosures. Aim for eight brief interviews per version. Ask visitors to explain the object's function, the supported consequence of its condition, what remains unknown, and why it merits attention; then collect a five-point discomfort rating and reason. Record preparation time. Stop and revise if two visitors describe the hypothetical task as documented history. Retain the concept only if it improves functional understanding and perceived significance over plain facts, and offers a useful gain over close observation without greater confusion or discomfort. Small samples support revision, not a general effectiveness claim.

EXPAND.title: Make the museum's choice accountable
EXPAND.proposal:
Use the case to explain a present curatorial decision: why exhibit this damaged everyday object? Interview the curator specifically about the reason for selecting it. Build a label of no more than 150 words around one defensible answer, such as its ability to demonstrate a construction feature recorded in the inspection notes. Attribute the judgment: “We selected this object because…” Include supported identification and condition, followed by: “Provenance and ownership history are unknown. The date and cause of the damage are unknown.” End with an optional question: “Does that reason justify giving this object space in a museum?” No response station is required.

The mechanism is accountable institutional valuation. A visitor can understand and contest the museum's reason for paying attention, rather than needing an undocumented biography to justify significance. This differs from the prior evidence-category route: the central issue is why the institution chose the object, rather than how certain individual claims are. It may also expose a weak selection rationale; that is a real limitation, not something to conceal through persuasive wording.

In week one, a staff lead uses the existing notes and curator interview to draft the rationale and verify every factual premise. The curator owns the final attribution. Proceed only if the curator can give an honest, object-specific reason supported by those materials. Do not imply rarity, representativeness, deliberate preservation, or historical exclusion without evidence. Install the object and printed label in the existing case, then reserve week two for comparison and revision. If no defensible rationale emerges, use the plain factual label. The route requires no acquisition history, additional research, or invented institutional backstory.
EXPAND.experiment: The staff lead compares this version with a plain factual label and the prior evidence-category label in balanced time blocks, aiming for eight visitor interviews per version. Keep established facts, provenance disclosure, legibility, and word limits equivalent. Ask visitors why the museum displayed the object, whether they personally find that reason convincing, and what is known about its past. Measure discomfort on a five-point scale and ask whether the wording felt pressuring or defensive. Record staff preparation time. Disagreement with the curator is not failure; inability to distinguish the curator's judgment from historical fact is. Stop and revise after two such confusions. Keep the approach only if visitors better understand a credible reason for display than with plain facts, with an advantage over evidence categories sufficient to justify the extra interview and drafting work. Report mixed reactions and the small sample's limits.

EXPAND.title: Improvement to P0: Close observation with a visibility gate
EXPAND.proposal:
Preserve P0’s mechanism: make the object meaningful by helping visitors discover something through its damage. Its strength is direct engagement with the object at low cost. Its blocking weakness is that a feature clear in inspection notes may be invisible through glass; the label then asks visitors to trust an assertion instead of making a discovery.

In week one, a staff lead selects one documented feature and checks it from ordinary visitor positions in the existing case. Use only an approved orientation and existing lighting. Ask the curator to verify both the observation and any explanation of construction or function. Do not infer affection, hardship, neglect, or the cause of damage.

The complete label, including its title, stays within 150 words. It gives supported identification, directs attention to the visible feature, explains one supported implication, and states: “Provenance and ownership history are unknown. The date and cause of the damage are unknown.” It ends by asking what the feature reveals about the object’s construction or ordinary use.

Proceed only if the feature is visible without moving or treating the object beyond approved arrangements. Otherwise install the plain factual label. This gate adds a short installation check but prevents the cost of compensating with increasingly elaborate interpretation. No new equipment or research is required. Compared with P1’s evidence categories, this route offers a more immediate material encounter, but depends more strongly on visibility.
EXPAND.experiment: In week two, the staff lead alternates the proposed and plain factual labels across four comparable short sessions, keeping object placement fixed; seek roughly 10 visitors per version. Ask each visitor what the damage helps them understand, what remains unknown, and their discomfort on a 0–4 scale, with an optional reason. Also ask them to locate the feature. Record unsupported historical claims and staff explanation requests. Stop and restore the factual label if the feature cannot reliably be located or the mounting raises a concern. Retain the concept only if answers suggest added understanding without greater discomfort or explanation burden; this small check cannot establish a population effect.

EXPAND.title: Improvement to P1: Evidence categories with a speculation gate
EXPAND.proposal:
Preserve P1’s mechanism: make the museum’s limits of knowledge meaningful. Its strength is explicit uncertainty with little installation work. Its weakness is that a “Possible” heading can give an attractive conjecture institutional authority, leaving visitors remembering a story that the museum cannot substantiate.

Replace the default three categories with two: “What we can establish” and “What remains unknown.” In week one, a staff lead extracts a few claims from the inspection notes and curator interview. The curator checks the basis of each. Include an interpretation only if its basis can be explained briefly beside it; otherwise omit it. This changes which claims enter the display, rather than merely adding a disclaimer after speculation.

Within 150 words, including headings, identify the object as far as supported, describe one documented damaged feature, and connect an established fact to construction or ordinary use where possible. Explicitly mark provenance and ownership history as unknown, along with any undocumented date or cause of damage. Place the object so visitors can inspect the cited feature. Do not imply that every uncertainty can be resolved.

The necessary prerequisite is at least one accessible, supported fact that contributes meaning beyond naming the object. If none emerges, use the plain factual label with an honest uncertainty statement. Compared with P0, this approach depends less on a visually striking feature but risks feeling administrative. The additional cost is a short claim review and potentially denser reading; it requires no additional objects, research, or technology.
EXPAND.experiment: During week two, the staff lead alternates this label with a plain factual label containing the same core facts and unknowns. Across four comparable sessions, seek approximately 10 responses per version. Ask visitors to explain one thing the object reveals and one thing the museum cannot establish; record whether they invent an owner or damage event. Collect a 0–4 discomfort rating and note reading abandonment and requests for explanation. Restore the factual label if the categories repeatedly cause confusion. Keep the revision only if visitors better distinguish evidence from uncertainty while retaining object-specific understanding, without an evident increase in discomfort or reading burden. Equal results would favor the simpler factual label.

EXPAND.title: New mechanism: The object’s future is a present choice
EXPAND.proposal:
Give the object significance through prospective stewardship: what should a museum retain when an everyday object is damaged? The mechanism is a present allocation of care, distinct from reconstructing its past, examining its damage, or explaining why it was selected. Visitors consider what future people could learn from keeping this particular object.

In week one, a staff lead asks the curator to identify one defensible reason for retaining the object in its current condition and one genuine limitation or cost of doing so. Use only information supported by the interview and inspection notes. The cost might concern interpretive limits or care requirements, but include neither unless actually established. Do not invent a proposed restoration, disposal decision, or institutional controversy.

The single case contains the object and a label totaling at most 150 words. Include supported identification and condition, explicitly state that provenance and ownership history are unknown, and mark undocumented causes and dates as unknown. Present the supported retention benefit and limitation, then ask: “What could someone learn from this object in the future that makes caring for it worthwhile?” Clarify that this is an invitation to reflect, not a binding collections decision. No response wall or visitor disclosure is needed.

This assumes the curator can articulate an object-specific future benefit and a genuine limitation. If either is missing, install the plain factual label. Staff must avoid implying that visitors are responsible for saving the object. Preparation uses the existing case, printed labels, notes, and interview; reserve week two for the comparison. Its upside is significance through responsibility, but it may shift attention from the object to museum policy or provoke guilt.
EXPAND.experiment: The staff lead alternates the stewardship and plain factual labels across four comparable sessions in week two, seeking about 10 visitors per version. Ask what makes this object worth attention, what is unknown about it, and discomfort on a 0–4 scale. Ask whether visitors felt pressured to endorse keeping it or believed an actual disposal decision was pending. Record object-specific answers versus generic statements about museums. Stop and restore the factual label if visitors repeatedly infer a real threat or obligation. Retain the concept only if it produces more grounded explanations of significance without increased discomfort, false historical beliefs, or pressure. The small trial may show no benefit and should not be presented as proof of superiority.
